## Force Direction Changes the Job {#sec-lay-ch09}

## A Concrete Picture

Push a shopping cart along its rolling direction and it can speed up. A sideways
push may turn it or be largely balanced by wheel reactions. A downward push can
change wheel loading without much forward acceleration. Direction changes the
interaction, but the motion follows the net force, moments, and constraints—not
one applied arrow in isolation.

At the grip, resolve a hand force along the shaft and along two transverse
directions. These components can load the shaft, accelerate the club center of
mass, and create a moment about that center. The moment depends on the force’s
line of action and chosen reference; a force applied at the hand has zero moment
about that same point. An independent grip moment is a separate load. As the club
rotates, a force fixed in the room changes its club-frame components. Direction
is a moving relationship, not a permanent assignment to translation or rotation.

![Hand-Force Components and the Moment Arm From the Club Center of Mass.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_force_direction.svg){#fig-lay-force-direction width=92% fig-alt="Along-shaft and transverse force components act at hand point H. A distinct center of mass G defines the moment arm from G to H; the hand force has zero moment about H itself."}

## How the Mechanism Works

Power begins with projection. The dot product $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v$ selects
the component of force along point velocity. Moment begins with a cross product,
$\mathbf r\times\mathbf F$, which selects the component perpendicular to the
moment arm. The same vector can therefore do little translational work yet create
a large moment, or deliver power through a moving base while its moment about a
particular point is small.

For the planar illustration, let $H$ be the hand point, $G$ the club center of
mass, $\hat e_s$ the shaft direction from grip toward head, and $\hat n$ a chosen
unit normal to the illustration plane. Define $\hat e_\perp=\hat n\times\hat e_s$.
Then $F_s=F\cdot\hat e_s$ and $F_\perp=F\cdot\hat e_\perp$; retain
$F_n=F\cdot\hat n$ in a spatial model. These are shaft-based components, not
automatically the normal and tangent of the hand or clubhead trajectory.

The force’s moment about $G$ is

$$M_G^{(F)}=(r_H-r_G)\times F.$$

In the straight-link idealization $r_G=r_H+\ell\hat e_s$, its projected moment
is $M_G^{(F)}\cdot\hat n=-\ell F_\perp$. Here $\ell$ is the hand-to-center-of-mass
distance, not necessarily the full club length. The figure labels the
center-to-hand lever arm $r_{GH}=r_H-r_G$. The minus sign follows the
stated basis. Its moment about $H$ is zero. Add any intrinsic grip moment
separately. A real club’s center of mass may lie off the shaft line, so even an
axial force can have a moment about $G$; use the actual vector lever arm.

Nor does an axial force automatically equal a centripetal requirement. For a
rigid offset $r_{HG}=r_G-r_H$, with angular velocity $\omega$ and angular
acceleration $\dot\omega$, the center acceleration is

$$\begin{aligned}
a_G={}&a_H+\dot\omega\times r_{HG}\\
&+\omega\times(\omega\times r_{HG}).
\end{aligned}$$

Hand acceleration and all external loads enter the balance. Only in a declared
fixed-center circular case does the inward net-force component reduce directly
to $m v^2/R$. An axial grip force can deliver positive power when the hand moves
along it, even when its moment about an on-axis center is zero.

### Vectors Rotate While Labels Stay Put

Suppose the laboratory vertical force remains upward through a short interval.
When the club is nearly horizontal, upward may be largely transverse to the
shaft. When the club is nearly vertical, upward may be largely axial. A plot of
global vertical force can remain positive while the signed shaft-transverse
component $F_\perp$ crosses zero.
Mechanistic claims should use the frame tied to the proposed job and provide the
transform back to measured coordinates.

@fig-lay-force-direction identifies the application point and moment arm.
The technical figures draw vectors on model snapshots because time traces alone
hide this geometry. At each selected phase, the reader can see force origin,
direction, scale, reference point, club orientation, and sign convention. A good
vector figure is an argument, not decoration.

### A Force Can Accelerate One Coordinate and Decelerate Another

Generalized coordinates need not be independent Cartesian directions. For a
specified force on a modeled body, virtual work gives $Q_H=J_H^T F_H$, where
$J_H$ maps generalized velocity to its application-point velocity. Include the
opposite interface load when the other body is also inside the modeled system.
Generalized forces are moments only for the corresponding angular coordinates.
After resolving ideal constraints, a contribution $Q_k$ produces
$\ddot q^{(k)}=M^{-1}Q_k$ at the same state in a nonsingular model. For example,
$M=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right]$ and
$Q_k=(1,0)^T$ give $\ddot q^{(k)}=(2/3,-1/3)^T$. Coupled response can have opposite
signs without violating action–reaction; it does not identify the source of
energy or muscle effort. Unreduced constrained equations require the associated
reaction solve, not an unconstrained inverse mass matrix.

The mass matrix then mixes generalized forces into accelerations. Looking only
at the sign of $F_\perp$ does not guarantee the sign of the relative wrist
acceleration $\ddot q_2$, where $q_2$ is the wrist angle relative to the arm
in the two-link example, when other terms are present. Exact decomposition solves the coupled equations at the same state
and reports the contribution rather than inferring it from one arrow.

### Direction Through the Downswing

Early in the downswing, the hand path and club orientation can make a large
reaction mostly along the shaft. Its path-radial role depends on the declared
center of curvature. Later, as relative
angle changes, a similar interaction can have a stronger tangential projection.
Near the impact zone, two separated hand forces may form a negative swing-normal
couple even while other pathways increase club kinetic energy.

This phase dependence is why the scientific question is not “is hand force good
or bad?” It is: which component, in which frame, over which interval, about which
reference point, with what power and impulse?

### Three Names for Parts of One Motion Equation

The double-pendulum model gives a more precise vocabulary for the forces that
appear as the arm turns and the wrist angle opens. It calls one contribution the
**Coriolis Cross Term**. This part contains the arm's rotation rate multiplied
by the wrist's relative opening rate. If either motion stops, the product is
zero. It is therefore a compact way to ask how simultaneous proximal rotation
and distal unfolding reshape the joint-coordinate balance.

A second contribution is the **Squared-Speed Term**: the collected terms
proportional to individual coordinate-rate squares in this registered model.
Curvature contributes to such terms, but this bin is not a measured inward
contact force. Centripetal describes an inward acceleration requirement in a
declared motion; centrifugal is an inertial term introduced in a rotating
observer’s equations. Those are different balance conventions. Do not add a
rotating-frame pseudo-force to an inertial free-body diagram that already
accounts for the motion.

Gravity supplies a third, configuration-dependent contribution. Unlike the
other two, it does not require motion. It can help or oppose the declared
coordinate depending on club orientation. Damping and applied moments complete
the model's account. Adding every declared contribution reproduces the modeled
acceleration; inventing a separate extra “centrifugal force” on top would count
the same mechanism twice.

These categories are coordinate-dependent. In this study the arm angle is
absolute and the wrist angle is relative to the arm. A different coordinate
choice can move algebra between cross-speed and squared-speed bins without
changing the physical trajectory. The full equations must transform together. Even the complete velocity-bias
vector is not independently invariant under a nonlinear coordinate change:
a free Cartesian particle $x=q^2$ has $\ddot x=0$, yet
$\ddot q=-\dot q^2/q$ for $q>0$. Its curved coordinate description introduces
a velocity term. Compare reconstructed physical accelerations and power, and
carry the coordinate and decomposition convention with every named contribution.

### Why an Outward Energy Story Needs More Than a Force Name

It is tempting to picture proximal energy as a parcel pushed outward by a
Coriolis force. The safer picture is a state being prepared. Earlier applied
moments and external forces build configuration and velocity. Once both links
are moving, geometry redirects the consequences of that stored motion through
the hinge. A Coriolis term can then make a large contribution even if the
instantaneous distal command is small. It did not create energy from nothing;
it describes how the moving system routes the effects of work already done and
work still entering.

The sign also needs care. The code reports each left-hand equation term and its
equal-and-opposite generalized drive. A positive equation term is not
automatically positive acceleration, and a large force impulse is not
automatically positive work. The drive must be paired with the appropriate
velocity to obtain power. This is why the source display shows impulse and work
side by side instead of giving one arrow a permanent “speed-producing” label.

### Normalization Can Hide Magnitude

Force arrows are often normalized for visibility. That communicates direction
but not magnitude. Other figures use one scale across all phases so arrow length
can be compared. Reports should say which convention is used. A tiny vector and
a huge vector drawn at equal length can otherwise invite a false mechanism.

Likewise, unit-body-mass normalization aids participant comparison but does not
restore missing contact allocation. Directional averages can cancel when
participants use different frames or handedness conventions. Preprocessing is
part of the interpretation.

**Model Result:** The archived planar double-pendulum audit reconstructs wrist
reaction from the links’ tangential/centripetal accelerations and gravity support.
That kinematic force balance is distinct from the coordinate-equation
Coriolis/squared-speed split. Both require the state and declared conventions;
neither alone identifies biological effort.
The two-hand geometric reconstructions test the separated-force couple under
frozen loads. They reverse that component under the stated transformations;
they do not necessarily reverse the entire grip moment or describe a new
forward trajectory.

**Human Evidence:** Net club motion alone does not uniquely identify both hand
wrenches. Additional measurements or explicit allocation assumptions are needed.
Koike’s single-instructor example used a strain-gauge handle with static
calibration, fixed contact points, and neglected handle-piece inertia
[@koike2016instrumented]. Choi and Park combined a six-axis internal-grip sensor
with inverse dynamics for nine right-handed male professionals. Their estimates
depend on the sensor/segment model; the heavier grip, hand overlap, and foam-ball
impact limit interpretation [@koike2020]. Neither study proves a passive human
control strategy. Rigid-body wrench conventions provide the mathematical
background [@featherstone2008].

**Hypothesis:** A late negative projected force couple can occur without an
instantaneous commanded free moment in a specified model. “Passive” must name
which commands and dissipative terms were removed, the retained state and stored
energy, and whether the result is a frozen-state evaluation or a new rollout.
Its sign alone proves neither passive muscles nor whole-system passivity.

**Practical Interpretation:** Replace “push harder” with a more scientific
question: where does the force point relative to the club, hand path, and desired
turning axis during that phase?

### The Same Force Can Do Different Jobs

Draw a force arrow at the grip. If its point of application is moving in the
same direction, the force delivers positive power. If motion is opposite, it
absorbs power. If motion is perpendicular, instantaneous translational power is
zero even though the force changes momentum direction. Rotate the club and the
same laboratory-frame force obtains different shaft-axis and transverse components.
No arrow has a permanent mechanical job independent of state.

This is why phrases such as “pulling on the handle” need coordinates. Pulling
toward the golfer, along the shaft, along the hand path, or opposite clubhead
motion are different vectors. A force can be inward relative to the clubhead
path but tangential relative to a joint. Resolve each vector in declared axes while retaining the same observer and
physical velocity. A common orthogonal axis rotation preserves a dot product.
Changing to an observer translating with velocity $U$ instead changes force
power by $-F\cdot U$. Distinguish a coordinate representation from a new
observer; the scalar work and energy balances must use matching conventions.

### Force at a Point Becomes a Wrench

A rigid body's external loading is summarized by a force and a moment at a
reference point. Move the reference point and the force remains the same while
the reported moment changes by the cross product of offset and force. This does
not change the physics. It changes the point about which the moment is reported.

Use net external force for center-of-mass translation. In body axes, spatial
rotation about the center obeys
$\sum M_G=I_G\dot\omega+\omega\times(I_G\omega)$, with constant body inertia
$I_G$. An arbitrary reference-point moment is not simply $I\dot\omega$;
a moving-point balance needs its transport terms.

For two contact forces $F_1,F_2$ at $r_1=c+d/2$ and $r_2=c-d/2$, define resultant
$R=F_1+F_2$ and differential force $D=(F_1-F_2)/2$. Include intrinsic
contact moments $C_1,C_2$. About a point with position $r_O$,

$$\begin{aligned}
M_O={}&(c-r_O)\times R+d\times D\\
&+C_1+C_2.
\end{aligned}$$

The separated-force couple is $d\times D$. The common-force moment vanishes at
the midpoint, but generally not at another reference point. Intrinsic moments can survive
when $d=0$. An axial differential load $D$ parallel to $d$ changes internal
loading while leaving both resultant force and force couple unchanged. Thus
net club loading cannot generally recover individual hand loading;
@sec-lay-ch12 examines the additional constraints and measurements needed.

### Following a Vector Through the Downswing

Early in the downswing, a large grip reaction may point largely along the club,
maintaining the curved path and transmitting proximal motion. Its direct
tangential acceleration contribution can be modest. As the club changes
orientation, the force’s shaft-axis components can change even if its
laboratory-frame components change smoothly. Late in the downswing, a smaller
force with a larger component perpendicular to the center-to-hand lever arm,
or a longer lever arm, may contribute a larger moment about the club center.

At the same time, hand-point velocity changes. Positive grip force power can
coexist with a negative swing-normal couple power because the translational and
rotational pieces differ. A complete display therefore shows the force vector,
moment vector, contact-point velocity, angular velocity, and the paired power
terms $F\cdot v$ and $M\cdot\omega$ at the same reference point. One scalar cannot represent this structure.

### A Geometry-Control Experiment

Take a simulated state and freeze its resultant $R$, differential force $D$,
midpoint $c$, and intrinsic moments. Reconstruct the force couple $d\times D$
under four controls: retain $d$; replace $d$ by $-d$ by swapping contact positions;
replace $D$ by $-D$; and shrink $d$ to zero. The force couple respectively stays
the same, reverses, reverses, and tends to zero **if the differential force $D$ remains bounded**.
Allowing $D$ to grow inversely with separation can keep the couple finite.
Neither the common-force moment about another reference point nor intrinsic contact
moments must vanish or reverse. Test the declared component, not a mislabeled
total wrench.

These controls are more informative than simply changing a force magnitude.
They challenge the proposed geometric pathway. If a nonzero separated-force
couple survives zero separation while $D$ remains bounded, the calculation or
labeling is wrong. A surviving intrinsic moment is
not such an error.
If the control behaves correctly, the model has passed a necessary mechanical
test but has not shown that golfers use that allocation.

### Measurement Frames Are Part of the Experiment

Instrumented grips report forces in sensor axes. Motion capture reports markers
in laboratory axes. The club carries a moving frame, while anatomical analysis
may use segment or joint frames. A calibration must locate each sensor and its
orientation relative to the club. Rotate force and moment components together,
and also transport moments when the reference point changes. Correct inertial
loads of sensor-side hardware when needed; a raw internal sensor wrench is not
automatically either hand’s complete wrench. Synchronize kinematics and loads
before combining them, then propagate both rotation and position uncertainty.

Small orientation errors can mix large axial forces into smaller transverse
components. Let $\delta$ be the sensor-axis misalignment angle. For one sign convention, a true axial/transverse pair of 100 N and
1 N becomes $1\cos\delta-100\sin\delta$ N transversely: at
$\delta=1^\circ$ it is about $-0.745$ N. The inferred sign reverses without a
physical force reversal. Such leakage can alter a moment’s swing-normal projection when that moment
depends on a small transverse force and its lever arm. Calibration uncertainty should therefore be propagated
into couple sign and timing, and reference transforms should be tested with
known loads before any biological interpretation.

### What a Useful Figure Should Show

A publication-grade force-vector figure should include coordinate axes,
reference point, hand locations, arrow scale, moment-arm line, phase or timestamp,
and sign convention. If arrows from different trials use automatic scaling, the
caption must say so. A sequence of frames should retain scale where comparison
matters. Accompanying plots should show components and resultant, not just one
selected direction.

For reviewers, the underlying numeric table should be linked. That makes it
possible to recalculate moments, transform frames, and verify that plotted
arrows match reported values. Visual intuition is valuable precisely when it is
anchored to auditable quantities.

### Questions That Keep the Claim Honest

Where is the force applied? About which point is moment calculated? In which
frame is “negative” defined? Is the vector measured, inferred, or simulated?
Does it do positive or negative power at that instant? Does reversing geometry
reverse the effect? Can another hand-force allocation produce the same net club
wrench? Answering these questions turns an arrow from decoration into evidence.

### Reader Lab: Verify a Two-Hand Diagram

Choose two three-dimensional hand positions and force vectors. Select a club
reference point. Compute net force and moment directly. Translate the reference
point and recompute; then verify total wrench power is unchanged for points on
the same rigid body, seen by the same observer, when the new point velocity is
transformed consistently. A cut through a deforming shaft or slipping interface
requires its own local velocity and energy balance. This catches the common mistake of
moving the moment without moving the velocity term.

Resolve each force in laboratory, club, and swing frames. Reconstruct the
original vector from every component set. Perturb sensor orientation by one or
two degrees and observe how much a large axial force leaks into the smaller
transverse component. Recompute the moment’s swing-normal projection; the
resulting change becomes part of sign uncertainty.

Animate the arrows through a simulated late downswing using one fixed scale.
Overlay moment arms and hand velocities. The visual should explain the calculated
couple and power rather than merely make forces look dramatic. Release the
numeric array so every arrow can be audited.

### Competing Force-Direction Stories

One hypothesis may say inward handle force changes club acceleration through
parametric geometry. Another may say a differential hand force supplies a
negative couple. A third may say shaft reaction explains the observed wrench.
They can coexist, but each predicts a different relationship among force
direction, hand motion, deformation, and state.

Separate algebraic checks from feasible dynamical interventions. Frozen-force
separation changes test the couple formula; alternative velocities paired with
the same force illustrate the power projection. Neither automatically supplies
a trajectory satisfying Newton’s laws and contact constraints. For a causal
comparison, reintegrate a declared model after changing geometry, compliance,
actuation, or controller while matching the initial state and reporting new
reactions. Removing shaft flexibility changes stored energy and often other
dynamics; specify what was matched. Compare those trajectories separately from
reconstructions so a correct cross product is not mistaken for a demonstrated
human mechanism.

## Where the Picture Breaks

The cart and planar arrows ignore distributed contact, three-dimensional axes,
and deformable tissue. The real grip force acts across an area; a six-axis sensor
reduces it to an equivalent wrench at a reference point. That reduction preserves resultant loading and, for a common rigid velocity
field, its power. It does not preserve local deformation work, contact pressure,
discomfort or tissue load without additional information.

Force direction alone also cannot identify muscle intent. The same hand wrench
can arise from many shoulder, elbow, wrist, and co-contraction patterns. Electromyography (EMG) adds
activation timing but not a unique force mapping.
